issues.legal_issue: Membership in an armed unlawful assembly with the common object of killing the victim may be established by the overall, corroborated evidence, without proof of a specific overt act by every member.
material_facts: Several eyewitnesses consistently described a large armed assembly attacking the victim and dragging him while members continued beating him.

One eyewitness specifically identified the appellants whose convictions were upheld, and other witnesses corroborated material parts of his account, including threats to intervening witnesses and the manner of the assault.
The eyewitness evidence was supported by the extensive injuries and medical evidence, and, for some appellants, by recovery of blood-stained weapons or clothing.

The appellants whose convictions were upheld had additional identifying evidence connecting them to the assembly, including participation in an earlier assault arising from the same dispute or corroboration by another witness.
issues.conclusion: The convictions of the five appellants whose participation was established beyond reasonable doubt were upheld. Once their membership in the unlawful assembly and its common object were established, proof of a particular overt act by each was unnecessary.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 141 and 149 IPC, formation of an unlawful assembly with the relevant common object permits liability to attach to its members for an offence committed in furtherance of that object; a specific overt act by each member need not be proved (Lalji v. State of U.P.). For a large assembly, evidence must be assessed for its quality and overall consistency: a wholly reliable single witness can suffice, though it is prudent to seek consistent support from more than one witness where many people witnessed the incident (Masalti v. State of U.P.; Chandra Shekhar Bind v. State of Bihar; Binay Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar). Consistency does not require every witness to repeat every accused’s name. A hostile witness’s testimony may be accepted to the extent it inspires confidence and is corroborated (Paulmeli v. State of Tamil Nadu), and relevant recovery evidence may be considered with the other evidence.

rule.if: appeal_from_conviction and armed_group_assault_established and common_object_to_kill_established and (credible_identification_corroborated or reliable_single_witness_identification)

predicates.appeal_from_conviction: The accused challenged a conviction on appeal.
predicates.armed_group_assault_established: Witnesses and other evidence established that a group armed with weapons jointly assaulted the victim.
predicates.common_object_to_kill_established: The circumstances of the assembly and the manner of the assault established that the group shared the object of killing the victim.
predicates.credible_identification_corroborated: A credible witness identified the accused as a group member, and material parts of that identification or account were corroborated by other evidence.
predicates.reliable_single_witness_identification: A single witness gave wholly reliable evidence identifying the accused as a member of the group.

issues.definition: If an appeal challenges a conviction and the evidence establishes an armed group assault and its common object to kill, a sufficiently reliable identification—corroborated or wholly reliable on its own—supports upholding group liability.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction for participation in an unlawful assembly cannot stand where the evidence does not reliably connect the accused to the assembly or the assault.
material_facts: For one appellant, the only name resembling his was an ambiguous name given by a witness, which the prosecution did not clarify; no other eyewitness identified him or other evidence connected him to the assembly.
For the other appellant, one witness named him, but no other eyewitness corroborated that identification or described any act connecting him to the assembly.
The weapons attributed to these appellants were not shown to carry blood stains, and the remaining evidence left reasonable doubt about their presence and participation.
issues.conclusion: The prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt against these two appellants. Their convictions were set aside and they were acquitted on benefit of doubt.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Evidence must be assessed for its quality and the accused’s individual connection to the assembly; an ambiguous or uncorroborated identification, unsupported by other connecting evidence, may leave reasonable doubt. Recovery of a weapon alone does not establish participation where the other evidence does not connect the accused to the crime.

rule.if: appeal_from_conviction and (identification_ambiguous or identification_uncorroborated) and no_independent_link_to_assembly

predicates.appeal_from_conviction: The accused challenged a conviction on appeal.
predicates.identification_ambiguous: The evidence identifying the accused was unclear or did not reliably establish that the witness meant that accused.
predicates.identification_uncorroborated: No other witness or material evidence adequately supported the identification of the accused as a participant.
predicates.no_independent_link_to_assembly: No other reliable evidence connected the accused to the assembly or the assault.

issues.definition: If an appealed conviction rests on an ambiguous or uncorroborated identification and no independent evidence links the accused to the group, the conviction is set aside and the accused is acquitted on benefit of doubt.

issues.legal_issue: A brutal group assault causing extensive injuries and death, carried out with the intention to kill, does not warrant reducing the murder conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
material_facts: A large assembly brutally beat the victim with blunt weapons and dragged him while the beating continued.
The victim sustained extensive injuries, including multiple fractures and injuries associated with rupture of the liver, and died from the resulting shock.
The court found that the manner in which the assembly carried out its object showed that its intention was to cause death.
issues.conclusion: The court rejected the request to alter the conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder and left the murder convictions undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied Section 300 IPC in assessing whether the killing amounted to murder, and Section 149 IPC in attributing the offence to members of the assembly. The extent and nature of the injuries, the continued beating while the victim was dragged, and the manner of the attack established an intention to cause death; the court found no basis to treat the case as culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

predicates.appeal_from_murder_conviction: The accused challenged a murder conviction on appeal and sought a lesser homicide conviction.
predicates.group_attack_caused_extensive_fatal_inju: A group assault caused extensive injuries that resulted in the victim’s death.
predicates.attack_manner_establishes_intent_to_kill: The manner of the group’s attack showed an intention to cause the victim’s death.

issues.definition: If an appeal challenges a murder conviction and the group attack caused extensive fatal injuries in a manner showing intent to kill, the conviction is not reduced to culpable homicide.
